name: Maltese
family: Afro-Asiatic, Semitic, Central Semitic, Arabic (descended from Siculo-Arabic), with heavy Italo-Romance and English contact
sources: Borg, Albert & Azzopardi-Alexander, Marie (1997). Maltese. London: Routledge.
Borg, Alexander (1997). Maltese phonology. In Alan S. Kaye (ed.), Phonologies of Asia and Africa, vol. 1, 245-285. Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns.
Vella, Alexandra (1994). Prosodic structure and intonation in Maltese and its influence on Maltese English. PhD dissertation, University of Edinburgh.

Vella, Alexandra (2003). Language contact and Maltese intonation: some parallels with other language varieties. In Kurt Braunmüller & Gisella Ferraresi (eds.), Aspects of Multilingualism in European Language History, 261-283. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.
Vella, Alexandra (2009). On Maltese prosody. In Bernard Comrie et al. (eds.), Introducing Maltese Linguistics, 47-68. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.
Grice, Martine, Vella, Alexandra & Bruggeman, Anna (2019). Stress, pitch accent, and beyond: intonation in Maltese questions. Journal of Phonetics 76: 100913.

Hume, Elizabeth, Venditti, Jennifer, Vella, Alexandra & Gett, Samantha (2009). Vowel duration and Maltese għ. In Bernard Comrie et al. (eds.), Introducing Maltese Linguistics. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.
Lucas, Christopher & Čéplö, Slavomír (2020). Maltese. In Christopher Lucas & Stefano Manfredi (eds.), Arabic and Contact-induced Change. Berlin: Language Science Press.
contrasts: vowel length: five short vowels against six long ones, the long ones in stressed syllables only
consonant gemination, word-medially and word-finally, for all consonants
voicing in obstruents, neutralised word-finally and in clusters
glottal stop /ʔ/ (written q) as a full consonant
one voiceless back fricative /ħ/ (written ħ, and h in some positions)
no emphatic consonants: the Arabic emphatics merged with the plain ones and left only vowel quality differences
/ts/ against /dz/ (both written z) and marginal /ʒ/ in recent loanwords
allophony: word-final obstruents are voiceless: kelb is [kɛlp], ħadd is [ħɐtt]
regressive voicing assimilation in obstruent clusters
/ħ/ varies between glottal, pharyngeal and velar or uvular voiceless fricative, between and within speakers
written għ has no consonantal value in most positions: it lengthens the neighbouring vowel (and may pharyngealise it); it is [ħ] word-finally and għ + h gives [ħħ]
written h is silent except word-finally, where it is [ħ]
voiceless stops are unaspirated or lightly aspirated; voiced stops are fully voiced; word-final stops may lack an audible release
/r/ is an alveolar tap or trill, for some speakers an approximant
nasals take the place of a following consonant
long vowels shorten when the stress moves off them
phonotactics: onsets of up to three consonants (skrivan, strixxa)
an initial geminate or an initial sonorant plus consonant cluster takes a prosthetic [ɪ] unless the preceding word ends in a vowel (imħabba, ikkanta)
long vowels occur in stressed syllables only

stress.type: weight-sensitive, one primary stress per word
stress.rule: Stress falls on the heavy syllable (long vowel or closed) nearest the end of the word within the last three syllables, except that a closed final syllable is stressed only if it is superheavy (long vowel plus consonant, or vowel plus two consonants); with no heavy syllable stress is penultimate (Vella 2009, as summarised by Grice, Vella & Bruggeman 2019).
stress.cues: duration (only stressed vowels can be long), pitch accent on accented words, intensity

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: long vowels shorten out of stress and unstressed short vowels are often lost through morphological syncope; vowels are not reduced to schwa
rhythm.notes: No rhythm-metric classification is cited here.

length.notes: Long vowels and geminates are written (double consonant letters; ie, and vowels next to għ or h) only in part. No duration ratios are given here; Hume et al. (2009) show that vowels next to għ are phonetically long.

intonation.declarative: falling nuclear configuration H*+L on the stressed syllable of the focus word, then a low phrase boundary; material after the focus is low with a final boundary tone
intonation.yes_no_question: word order of a statement; rising nuclear configuration, low accent L* on the stressed syllable of the focus word followed by a high phrase boundary
intonation.wh_question: a very high peak at the left edge of the question word, higher than the peaks of other sentence types and not tied to its stressed syllable, then a fall to a low stretch
intonation.continuation: high boundary at the end of each non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: H*+L: high on the stressed syllable, falling into the next one
intonation.notes: After Vella (1994, 2003, 2009) and Grice, Vella & Bruggeman (2019). Late-focus statements resemble Palermo Sicilian, question-word questions Tuscan Italian, and yes-no questions the Arabic dialects (Vella 2003).

tone.notes: No lexical tone; all tones are post-lexical.

phonation: vowels next to written għ may be pharyngealised

problems: mt_rules is a stub. Several consonant letters are given a following vowel as if they were spelled: d gives [de], k [ke], x [ʃe], z [tse], ż [zə], ċ [tʃə]. So dar gives [dear], xemx gives [ʃeˈemʃe], ħobż gives [hobzˈə], ċavetta gives [tʃəavˈetːa].
q, the glottal stop /ʔ/, is dropped before a vowel and turned into a stressed schwa elsewhere: qalb gives [alp], triq gives [trɪˈə].
ħ is the glottal [h] of the base table, and there is no [ħ] for word-final h or għ.
j is read as the vowels [iu] and w as [u]: żejt gives [zeiut], għajn gives [aiun].
z is always [tse] with a vowel; /dz/ and /ʒ/ are missing.
ie is [iː] or [iˈə] instead of [ɪː]; vowels after r, k and n are lengthened by rule whatever the word (mara gives [maraː]), so written length and spoken length do not agree.
Stress is penultimate for every word, and the explicit stress marks inside some rules (be, bie, q) override it; final superheavy syllables are not stressed.
The vowel table is copied from another language: it contains front rounded vowels and their diphthongs and lacks the Maltese qualities [ɐ] and [ɪː].
good: word-final devoicing is on: kelb gives [kelp]
ġ, ċ and x map to dʒ, tʃ and ʃ

notes: Maltese needs a full set of letter-to-sound rules before the phonetic detail matters: nearly every test word came out wrong.
